/SUNDAY THROUGH THURSDAY/... 
A significant weather event could be shaping up for next Monday
into Tuesday as models are beginning to come to a better 
consensus for a seasonably strong upper level trough moving 
through our region. The biggest uncertainty still involves how 
much moisture will be available when the trough does move through,
but it is looking more optimistic compared to last night. 

This next event is expected to start with strong upper level
moisture advection from the southwest which will actually come
from the remnants of the decaying tropical system Odalys. Odalys
is forecast to drift northward over the next day or two before
getting absorbed into the westerlies as a trough digs
southeastward off the coast of California. We can anticipate
plenty of higher level moisture and clouds overspreading our area
beginning Saturday evening and continuing through much of Sunday.
This moisture fetch is likely to be very consistent for 18-24
hours with gradual top-down moistening of the atmosphere. By
Sunday mid to late morning, some areas may start to see some
sprinkles, or even very light rain, but no measurable rainfall. It
would not be surprising to see a fairly narrow band of light rain
developing by Sunday evening somewhere across the area, but
amounts are expected to remain very light. 

Also starting Sunday, Hurricane Polo is forecast to approach
southern Baja before eventually tracking to the northeast across
Baja and the Gulf of California most likely later on Monday. The
latest NHC track of Polo keeps it well to our south as it is
expected to fall apart quickly as it moves onshore into southern
Sonora Mexico. We are not worried about any direct impacts from
Polo, but it is becoming increasingly more likely it will help
direct additional moisture northward into our region, specifically
in the low to mid levels. This moisture will be necessary for any
decent rainfall to occur early next week, so any big deviations in
the forecast moisture will affect our rain chances for Monday and
Tuesday.

Although the details are expected to change, forecast confidence
for a decent weather/rain event continues to increase. As the bulk
of the upper level moisture from the remnants of Odalys mostly 
pushes into New Mexico later on Sunday, we should begin to see 
moisture stream out of the south southwest from Polo by Monday 
morning. The best moisture is expected to bypass our region to the
southeast, but we still should see good moisture working into 
most of Arizona early on Monday, right ahead of the approaching 
upper level trough. Ensemble mean PWATs of 200% of normal are 
shown for the eastern 2/3rds of Arizona on Monday with the bulk of
this moisture falling in the low and mid levels, just where it 
would be needed for a decent rain event. 

The upper level trough will play a very important role early next
week as it looks likely to provide strong forcing on Monday and 
Tuesday. Upper level ascent is expected to be quite good, along 
with very good 30-45 kts of southwesterly upslope forcing within 
the mid levels. It is still too early to have a great idea on the 
details of the evolution of the rainfall, but it could start in 
earnest by Monday morning. NBM PoPs increase areawide by Monday 
morning with 30-50% chances across the western deserts to 50-75% 
from Phoenix and north and east of Phoenix. These PoPs basically 
hold through Monday night before gradually tapering off from west 
to east on Tuesday. We may see fairly steady upslope showers and 
isolated thunderstorms across south-central and eastern Arizona 
Monday through early Tuesday.

We are currently looking at three possible scenarios for early
next week. First, and the most likely outcome (~60% chance), is 
for a modestly strong upper level trough to push through Monday 
into Tuesday with very adequate, but not tropical level moisture 
getting pulled into our area right ahead of the passing trough. 
This scenario would support widespread rainfall amounts of 
0.10-0.30" over the lower deserts to 0.5-1.0" over the high 
terrain north and east of Phoenix. This should also involve a 
period of strong thunderstorms due to quite good wind shear. 
Second, (~20% chance) would keep the best moisture to our south 
and/or a much weaker and faster trough. In this scenario, we would
expect much more scattered rainfall with lower desert amounts 
under a 0.25" and higher terrain amounts more like 0.25-0.75". At 
the other end of the spectrum (~20% chance) would leave us with 
the upper end of potential moisture combining with a stronger and 
slower trough. This would bring a longer rain event with lower 
desert rain amounts averaging from 0.2-0.5" over the western 
deserts to 0.75-1.50" for the south-central Arizona lower deserts.
As much as 2-3" would also be very possible over the high terrain
north and east of Phoenix. This stronger event is also likely to 
involve a period of strong to severe storms.
